title: Pocket priming & soft-backstop notes
content:
Goal: lightweight, low-risk way to reduce early-run variance for small-cohort releases (soft-backstop) so client-facing latencies and cost spikes are minimized during first 1–6 hours. This is a personal lab notebook for tactics I want to try before making a product PR.

Background/context:
- We've seen bursty 95p latency and token cost during initial ramp for micro-cohorts (0.1%–2%) when cold caches + long-tail KV warmups align with complex prompts.
- Full warmup (traffic soak) is expensive and noisy for customers; want an intermediate approach that is cheaper than full soak but reduces the tail.
- Idea: "pocket priming" - targeted, short-lived synthetic priming against a small representative subset of tenants/clients and paths, combined with a soft-backstop that holds a tiny reserve of capacity and an auto-pin fallback for the first 30–90 minutes.

Experiment sketch (first pass):
- Target cohort: 50 internal test clients + 10 canary customers (opt-in). Total real traffic ~0.05% of prod.
- Prime sequences: 3 patterns per model (short/medium/long). Each pattern uses canonical prompts from eval set + 5 high-KV prompts from recent client logs.
- Priming cadence: every 30s for first 15 minutes, then every 2m for next 45 minutes. Stop after 60 minutes.
- Synthetic concurrency: at most 5 parallel priming requests per node to avoid bumping real traffic.
- Budget: ~2000 priming tokens per node for m-7 sequence length distribution; estimate cost ~0.2% additional token spend for cohort.

Safety and rate control:
- priming-tag header so traffic is visible in Console and billing (easy to subtract).
- enforce priming requests to low-priority queue with strict preemption in router policy.
- if node CPU/GPU utilization > 60% or p95 latency delta > +15% on real requests, pause priming for 10 min and re-evaluate.

Soft-backstop behaviors (auto-safety):
- Hold a small reserved pool: 2 GPUs per region marked soft-backstop for first 90m after rollout. These are kept for canary traffic and fast fallback.
- If real request p50/p95 degrade beyond thresholds (p95 > baseline * 1.35 OR error rate +0.6%), route affected keys to pinned model variant (smaller quantized) automatically.
- Rollback trigger threshold: sustained violation > 6min AND gradient increasing for 3 consecutive 1m windows.

Telemetry & signals to watch (quick queries):
- per-route p95 and p99 (1m and 5m), tokens per request histogram, prefix hit-rate, kv-cache-miss-rate.
- KPI query examples to run in Console: 
  * SELECT p95 FROM latency WHERE route = 'chat' AND cohort = 'canary' SINCE 10m
  * SELECT count(*) FILTER(error) GROUP BY tenant SINCE 5m
- Add a temporary Canary dashboard with these 6 tiles: p50 p95 p99, error-rate, token-cost-per-request, kv-cache-hit.

Post-deploy checklist (for me):
- [ ] Upload priming patterns to S3 and add manifest to runtime config (bucket path + timestamp).
- [ ] Create temporary canary cohort in Console and add 10 customer ids.
- [ ] Schedule priming job with runbook id and Slack notification to #release-watch.
- [ ] Enable soft-backstop pool for target regions.
- [ ] Start observers: Ivy on telemetry, Mateo on routing hooks.
- [ ] Hold 30m quiet window immediately after start (no config changes).

Draft runbook steps (condensed):
1) PREP: verify manifests, confirm reserved pool in console, set priming TAG.
2) START: kick priming with low concurrency. Send Slack summary: model, cohort, expected spend, abort criteria.
3) WATCH: 0–30m, check p95/p99 every 5m, be ready to pause priming if thresholds cross.
4) SOFT-FALLBACK: if triggered, auto-pin affected tenant(s) to "q4-small" model variant and notify release channel.
5) PAUSE/RESUME: use pause for priming if utilization/latency spikes; resume with 50% cadence after 10m.
6) TEARDOWN: after 60–90m, stop priming and decommission soft-backstop pool unless extended run approved.

Quick heuristics/notes from small dry runs:
- Observed median p95 drop of 7–12% on routes with prime-matched prompts when priming ran for 30m in lab. Not universal; effectiveness tied to prompt similarity.
- Too-aggressive priming (high concurrency) introduced contention on nodes serving low-traffic tenants -> added jitter and more variability. Keep concurrency low.
- Prefix-caching helps most when the model uses long context (>1024) and when hot prompts are stable.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How to generalize priming manifest generation? (scriptable from eval sets vs. recent logs)
- Should priming traffic come from actual SDK clients (real requests flagged) or synthetic runner? Pros/cons: realism vs. client billing confusion.
- Need an easy Console toggle to mark reserved soft-backstop GPUs and auto-rollback policies. Raise product ticket?
- What's acceptable spend threshold for customers? We should expose an opt-out for customers to avoid being used for synthetic priming.

Next steps (short):
- Iterate priming manifest sampler to pick diverse prompts (Mateo).
- Prototype a CLI runbook to start/stop priming with guardrails (Ivy).
- Draft a Confluence note outlining policy for customer opt-in/opt-out and token accounting.

Notes-to-self: keep this intentionally small and reversible. If priming helps reduce tail without adding noise, bake into canary flow; otherwise shelve. When writing product PR, include clear billing attribution, and a config flag per org to disable synthetic priming.

References and quick links:
- Confluence design (linked above) contains ideas on manifest format and pinned variants.
- Jira: INFR-4212 is the tracking ticket for the priming experiment.
- Runtime PR: see linked GH PR for initial routing preemption hook.

End of notebook entry.

-- SK
